catalog_quote: Hyman 1979: 12: "The Aghem language has two basic level tones, H (high) and L (low) which are represented, respectively, by an acute (’) and a grave (') accent. Since tone is assumed to be a property of the syllable in this language, only one tone mark is written per syllable (even if there is a long vowel, which is written double)". Hyman 1979: 2: "an Aghem stem syllable carries one of two contrasting basic or underlying tones (high or low)". Watters 1979: 140: "Aghem is a tone language." Attia 2004: 77: "Unlike in Aghem where the tone is unpredictable, as it is a property of the syllable and therefore is in the underlying representation (unless it can be shown that such a given tone is the result of H tone or Low tone spreading), the tones in the Aghem borrowed words from English are determined by the stress in word. The Aghem speakers match stressed syllables in English with High tones and unstressed syllables with low tones."
world_status: statement found in an open source

Quote check: (a) Hyman "an Aghem stem syllable carries one of two contrasting basic or underlying tones (high or low)" is present verbatim but sits at the top of book p. 2 (p. 14, sentence begins "Finally, as will be discussed in chapter 2.."), not on p. 1 as the locator says — the only discrepancy; (b) Hyman p. 12 (p. 24, §2.1 Surface tones) "The Aghem language has two basic level tones, H (high) and L (low) which are represented, respectively, by an acute and a grave accent. Since tone is assumed to be a property of the syllable in this language, only one tone mark is written per syllable" — v…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Aghem is a two-tone language (H vs. L, lexically contrastive on every syllable; plus L°, downstep, downdrift, floating tones and HL/LH contours). Almost all lexical stems are monosyllabic, with tonal prefixes/suffixes. No word stress is described or mentioned in the primary grammar. The only statement involving stress is Attia's loanword observation: English word stress is reinterpreted as H tone (stressed syllable -> H, unstressed -> L), which implies Aghem has no independent stress system of its own.
new_statements.exceptions: Attia 2004: 78 notes the stress-to-H mapping in loans is not absolute — an unstressed English syllable may still receive H in Aghem (e.g. 'driver'). Hyman notes the LH rising tone is rare and mostly limited to long vowels; downstep is unpredictable in isolation forms ('rat' vs 'foot').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on syllables, illustrated on citation forms (nouns and infinitives in isolation) and in phrases; downdrift/downstep and L° vs falling L operate at phrase/pre-pause level. Attia's stress statement concerns the adaptation of English words only.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1979 describes Aghem proper (ALCAM 810, the language of Wum; data from speaker Timothy Inah Buo, per the preface), i.e. aghe1239; Attia 2004 is by a native speaker of Aghem. Neither treats the related Aghem-cluster varieties (Weh, Isu, Zhoa, Bu, which have their own glottocodes) — Thormoset 2007 covers those comparatively. No dialect issue.

new_statements.quote: Anderson p. 77: "As is common for Bantu languages, verb roots can be assigned to one of two tone classes: either "High" (H) or "Low" (L). In Aghem, some of the minimal pairs which establish this distinction are cited below". Watters p. 190, note 3: "Note that Aghem does not exploit the phonological structures of the language to mark a focused constituent, as is done in English, for example. Thus, Aghem is one of numerous tone languages in the world which mark the focus by non-phonological means."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tone language, no stress statement' from Hyman ch. 1-2 (pp. 1-15). Adds: (i) the verb lexicon is also organised in H vs L tone classes (Anderson p. 77, appendix of 204 verbs), (ii) Watters p. 190 n. 3 states that Aghem does not use phonological means (stress/intonation) to mark focus, i.e. no prosodic prominence even at the phrase level for focus. Neither remaining part states where word stress falls or that stress exists; the pages named in the work entry (Hyman 16-72, Anderson 73-136) are silent on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Aghem is a two-level tone language (H and L) with downdrift and downstep; noun stems and verb roots belong to H or L tone classes, and Anderson's ch. 8 gives the verb-phrase tone rules (spreading, prefix-deletion, downstep, simplification of rising tones, tone replacement). Nothing in the volume describes word stress or any stress-like prominence; the only prominence remark is Watters' note that focus is marked by word order, verbal morphology, the particle no and clefts, not by stress or intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule is stated, so no exceptions).
new_statements.identity_note: The volume describes the Aghem of Wum: Watters note 1, p. 190 (PDF 202): "Aghem is spoken in the North West Province of Cameroon, primarily in the town of Wum." No other dialect is distinguished in the pages read.

Southern California Occasional Papers in Linguistics 7. Los Angeles: Dept. of Linguistics, USC. xii+218 pp. Part I Hyman 'Phonology and noun structure' pp. 1-72 (ch. 1 The sound system pp. 1-11; ch. 2 The tone system pp. 12-15); Part II Anderson 'Verb structure' pp. 73-136; Part III Watters 'Focus in Aghem' pp. 137-197.
sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent anywhere in ch. 1 (syllable structure, consonants, vowels, final VC constraints, phonological rules) or ch. 2 (tone system). Describes Aghem as having two basic level tones H and L, tone a property of the syllable, plus L°, downstep, downdrift, floating tones and HL/LH contours (pp. 1, 12-15). Watters p. 140: 'Aghem is a tone language.' The only 'stress' in the scanned pages is Watters' English example sentence (p. 140). Preface and Anderson ch. 1 also silent.

sources.note: Historical-comparative phonology of Aghem, Bu, Isu, Weh, Zhoa (segments and vowels); no synchronic statement on Aghem stress or accent. sources.citation: Attia, Lilian Mbi. 2004. Borrowing and standardization in Aghem. Maîtrise thesis, Université de Yaoundé I, Dept. of African Languages and Linguistics. x+124 pp.
sources.note: §1.3.1.3 Tones (pp. 15-17): two basic tones H and L, one tone per syllable, tones lexically contrastive; no stress mentioned there. §3.1.13.1 'On stressed words' (pp. 77-78): Aghem tone is lexically unpredictable, but in English loanwords tone is determined by English word stress: stressed syllables map to H, unstressed to L (with exceptions, e.g. 'driver' where an unstressed syllable also gets H). By a native speaker.
